strapline: A flash disk stalls the treason bail hearing until Friday; Jay Jay Banda too ill to be produced; debt at US$30.89 billion; and the under-23s lose in Ouagadougou

stories.title: A flash disk, five paragraphs and a second objection: the treason bail hearing stalls again, and the court rules on Friday whether the raid video stays on the record
stories.excerpt: A day after losing its first preliminary objection, the State raised another at the Lusaka High Court on Wednesday 11 November, asking the three-judge panel to strike five paragraphs and a video recording from the affidavit filed by Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 16 co-accused. The defence says the footage shows the raid on Zulu's home and answers the State's flight-risk claim. The court adjourned to 11:00 on Friday 13 November to rule, then hear the bail plea. In the sedition case, The Zambian Observer reported that the two dismissed their lawyers.

image.label: The flash disk objection
image.caption: The State wants a video and five paragraphs removed from the bail record; the court will say on Friday 13 November whether they stay.

body: The constitutional bail application by the defeated presidential candidate Brian Mundubile, his running mate Makebi Zulu and 16 other people charged with treason was supposed to be argued on Wednesday 11 November. Instead the day was spent on a new preliminary objection. The Director of Public Prosecutions, Gilbert Phiri, asked the Lusaka High Court to strike out five paragraphs and a video recording from the applicants' affidavit in reply, Zambia Monitor reported on Thursday morning, and the three-judge panel adjourned to 11:00 on Friday 13 November to rule on that request and, if it can, to hear the bail application itself.

The objection came a day after the same panel, Justices Derrick Mulenga, Davies Chibwili and Ireen Wishimanga, dismissed the State's first preliminary objection, which had argued that the application was begun in the wrong form. News Diggers, which carried the defence lawyer Sakwiba Sikota's account on Thursday, reported that the State's new position is that the applicants raised fresh issues in their affidavit in reply on which it had not been allowed to respond.

According to The Zambian Observer, which carried a TV Yatu report on Wednesday afternoon, the footage shows a shoot-out during a raid on Mr Zulu's residence, and the defence filed it to answer the State's argument that the accused are a flight risk because they allegedly evaded arrest, including by seeking shelter at United Nations premises. The defence's position, as Mr Sikota put it, is that the applicants went to the UN because they feared for their lives, and that this should not count against them in a bail decision. He said the substantive hearing could only start once the preliminary issues were disposed of.

body.text: It seems they [State] are very uncomfortable with the flash disk.
body.attribution: Sakwiba Sikota, lawyer for the applicants, speaking outside court on Wednesday 11 November, as quoted by The Zambian Observer

body: Zambia Monitor set out the legal arguments in more detail. The State questioned the authenticity, origin and integrity of the recording and cited Section 9 of the Electronic Communications and Transactions Act, together with the case of OTK Limited v Amanita Zambia Limited and Others, to argue that electronic evidence must be authenticated before it is admitted. The applicants answered that the disputed paragraphs respond directly to the State's flight-risk claim and that doubts about authenticity go to the weight of the evidence, not to whether it can be received. Mr Zulu, who is representing himself as the second applicant, argued that the affidavit had been properly sworn before a Commissioner for Oaths, that the State's demands belong to oral testimony at trial rather than affidavit proceedings, and that a flash disk is a document under the Evidence Act. The panel observed that the matter is a constitutional case with criminal implications before adjourning.

The Observer's earlier report on Wednesday said the hearing had been listed for 09:00 and that the Attorney General, Mulilo Kabesha, had asked for an adjournment because of another court commitment. The 18 applicants have been in custody since 14 August over alleged treason, sedition and terrorism-related offences, the Observer reported; they have sued Mr Kabesha and Mr Phiri, arguing that their continued detention breaches their constitutional rights, and are asking for unconditional release or bail on reasonable conditions.

body.text: The sedition case, and the lawyers

body: Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu were also due before the Lusaka Magistrate's Court on Wednesday in the seditious practices case transferred from Solwezi. The Daily Nation reported that proceedings did not start in the morning because the two accused were required at the High Court, and that the matter was pushed to 12:00. The Zambian Observer reported on Wednesday evening that the two men had dismissed their lawyers in that case and asked for ten minutes before taking plea; its short report, built around a Zambian Watch video, did not say why the lawyers were let go or who will now represent them, and no other outlet read for this edition had confirmed the detail by Thursday morning. The sedition case alleges that the two declared themselves winners of the August election before the Electoral Commission of Zambia announced the result; that is the State's allegation, and the case has not been tried. Their bail application in the sedition case was adjourned on Monday to Monday 16 November, the Observer reported on Wednesday morning.

The Observer also carried a statement on Wednesday by the governance activist Laura Miti, who placed the detentions in a line that runs from the 1993 Zero Option arrests through Kenneth Kaunda's 1997 detention to Hakainde Hichilema's own treason arrest in 2017, and said the State should either bring substantive charges to trial or release the accused. The State's position in court, as reported by the Observer, is that the detentions are lawful and that the accused are flight risks.

body.title: What happens on Friday
items: **11:00, Lusaka High Court** — ruling on the State's application to strike five paragraphs and the video from the affidavit in reply.
**If the objection fails or is disposed of** — the constitutional bail application can finally be argued.
**Monday 16 November, Lusaka Magistrate's Court** — the adjourned bail hearing in the sedition case.

body.confirmed: That the State raised a second preliminary objection on Wednesday 11 November seeking to strike five paragraphs and a video from the applicants' affidavit in reply, that the applicants opposed it, and that the court adjourned to 11:00 on Friday 13 November to rule and then hear the bail application — from Zambia Monitor, News Diggers and The Zambian Observer. That the sedition proceedings were pushed to midday on Wednesday — from the Daily Nation.
body.unverified: What the video actually shows: the defence's description of a raid and shoot-out at Mr Zulu's residence has not been tested, and the State disputes its authenticity. The report that the two dismissed their lawyers in the sedition case rests on The Zambian Observer alone, and the reasons are not known. All 18 are presumed innocent; treason and sedition are allegations the State must prove.

stories.title: Ordered to court at nine, not produced: the State says Jay Jay Banda's doctor will not let him leave Maina Soko, and the judge demands a medical report before Friday
stories.excerpt: Judge Geoffrey Mulenga had ordered the State to bring the former Petauke Central MP Emmanuel Jay Jay Banda before the Lusaka High Court at 09:00 on Wednesday 11 November to explain the circumstances of his detention. He was not brought. The Attorney General's office said the doctor treating him at Maina Soko Military Medical Centre had not authorised his movement, and the judge ordered a medical report. The court is expected to rule on Friday on whether the habeas corpus hearing moves to the hospital.

image.label: Habeas corpus, day one
image.caption: A writ that is meant to put a detained person in front of a judge has so far produced a request for a doctor's note.

body: The habeas corpus application brought by the mother of Emmanuel Jay Jay Banda reached the Lusaka High Court on Wednesday 11 November without the man it concerns. Judge Geoffrey Mulenga had directed on Tuesday that the State produce the former Petauke Central MP at 09:00 the next morning to explain the circumstances of his apprehension and detention, News Diggers reported on Tuesday evening. On Wednesday the State did not do so, and the judge ordered the Attorney General, Mulilo Kabesha, to produce a medical report on Mr Banda's condition instead, News Diggers and The Zambian Observer reported.

The State's explanation, as reported by both outlets, is that the doctor attending to Mr Banda at Maina Soko Military Medical Centre had not authorised his movement. News Diggers, quoting a defence lawyer, reported that when the case came up in chambers Mr Kabesha applied for the proceedings to be held at Maina Soko itself, and that the court is expected to rule on Friday, after reading the medical report, on whether the hearing should move there. The Observer said the judge wanted the report in order to understand why Mr Banda remained absent.

The application was filed on 30 October by Grace Nampokolwe Banda, who is asking for a writ of habeas corpus ad subjiciendum over her son's continued detention, News Diggers reported. In her affidavit she said she had made repeated attempts to establish his whereabouts and status without success, that her lawyers had been instructed to approach the Inspector General of Police, and that she believed he was being held at an undisclosed location, raising concerns about his welfare and the lawfulness of the detention.

The Daily Nation, previewing Wednesday's hearing, reported that Mr Banda was reportedly captured in Mozambique by State agents and had been at Maina Soko for more than a month, and that his mother told the court she had not had access to him since he was brought back to Zambia on 14 October and that the State had declined to disclose his whereabouts or condition. Police confirmed on 16 October that he had been apprehended and was in the country awaiting formal arrest and charging, News Diggers reported; none of this week's reports records a charge having been laid since.

A habeas corpus application asks a court to compel those holding a person to bring him before it and justify the detention. Wednesday's order does not decide the lawfulness of Mr Banda's detention; it only asks the State to show, in writing, why he cannot be brought to court. Friday's ruling will decide whether the court goes to him.

body.confirmed: That the State did not produce Mr Banda on Wednesday 11 November, citing his doctor; that Judge Mulenga ordered a medical report; and that a ruling on holding the hearing at Maina Soko is expected on Friday — from News Diggers and The Zambian Observer. That the application was filed on 30 October by his mother — from News Diggers.
body.unverified: Mr Banda's actual condition, the reason he is at a military hospital, where and how he was apprehended (the Daily Nation reports Mozambique), and whether any charge has been laid. The State has not been reported giving an account of the apprehension in court.

stories.title: US$30.89 billion owed, US$275 million saved: external debt fell 5% after the Eurobond buyback, Musokotwane tells Parliament, as the IMF board weighs a US$1.46 billion programme
stories.excerpt: Central government debt stood at US$30.89 billion at the end of June 2026, split almost evenly between domestic and external borrowing, the Finance Minister told the National Assembly on Tuesday 10 November. External debt fell from US$16.15 billion in December to US$15.35 billion, mainly because the Treasury bought back about US$1.36 billion of its 2053 Eurobond in May at a discount. A staff-level agreement on a new 36-month IMF programme worth US$1.46 billion was reached on 9 October; the Fund's board is expected to decide in December.

image.label: US$30.89 billion
image.caption: Domestic borrowing now slightly exceeds external debt, and the next IMF decision is a board vote pencilled in for December.

body: Zambia's central government debt was US$30.89 billion at the end of June 2026, the Minister of Finance and National Planning, Situmbeko Musokotwane, told Parliament on Tuesday 10 November. Of that, US$15.54 billion was domestic debt and US$15.35 billion external, Zambia Monitor, News Diggers and The Zambian Observer all reported. The external figure is about 5% lower than the US$16.15 billion recorded at the end of December 2025, a fall the minister attributed mainly to a liability management operation early this year linked to a Eurobond buyback, together with slower disbursements on external loans.

The buyback itself was done in May 2026, Zambia Monitor reported: the government repurchased roughly US$1.36 billion of its Bond B, which had been due to mature in 2053, at below the bond's original value. The Treasury puts the saving at an estimated US$275 million and has earmarked it for the Energy Grid Resilience Programme, News Diggers reported. Dr Musokotwane told the House that a Special Report with fuller detail would be laid before Parliament and that further consolidation of the country's bonds is planned under a Benchmark Bond Policy. He said the government remained firmly committed to debt sustainability.

The minister's statement also set out where the relationship with the International Monetary Fund stands, Zambia Monitor reported. The previous 38-month Extended Credit Facility, approved on 31 August 2022, was completed on 27 January 2026 with about US$1.7 billion drawn. A staff-level agreement on a successor ECF was reached on 9 October 2026: 36 months, US$1.46 billion, split equally between balance-of-payments support and budget support. That is not final approval; the IMF Executive Board is expected to consider the programme in December 2026.

The remarks came in answer to a supplementary question from the Lukashya MP, Daniel Bwalya of the NRPUP, who asked which African country had seen people's lives improve after an IMF programme, News Diggers reported. Dr Musokotwane's reply was that Zambia itself was an example of a country that had become better off.

body.text: itself is an example of a country that has become better off
body.attribution: Situmbeko Musokotwane, Minister of Finance and National Planning, on Zambia, answering a supplementary question in the National Assembly on Tuesday 10 November, as quoted by News Diggers

body: The Secretary to the Treasury, Felix Nkulukusa, gave the growth side of the same argument at the 2027 budget symposium on Monday 9 November, News Diggers reported: Zambia can reach an US$80 billion economy by 2031 if it hits the growth targets that begin with the 2027 budget, and domestic revenue is expected to reach 23.6% of GDP by 2029. Dr Musokotwane told the symposium that policies and regulations must change so that the private sector drives export-led growth.

body.title: The debt numbers, as reported
items: **Total central government debt, end-June 2026** — US$30.89 billion.
**Domestic** — US$15.54 billion. **External** — US$15.35 billion, down from US$16.15 billion in December 2025.
**May 2026 buyback** — about US$1.36 billion of Bond B (due 2053), estimated saving US$275 million.
**Successor ECF** — staff-level agreement 9 October; 36 months; US$1.46 billion; board decision expected December 2026.

stories.title: K12,253.72 to keep a Lusaka family of five: the JCTR basket jumps K854 in a month, and the centre says the budget should have taxed copper windfalls, not wage earners
stories.excerpt: The Jesuit Centre for Theological Reflection's Basic Needs and Nutrition Basket for Lusaka rose 7.5% in October, from K11,399.64 to K12,253.72, driven by vegetables and bananas in the hot season. Its director, Fr Daniel Mutale, says formal workers already carry the heaviest tax load and that the budget's VAT and mobile-money increases will reach the poor; PwC, meanwhile, says households will feel the budget at the till and wants a timetable for K60 billion in unpaid VAT refunds.

image.label: K12,253.72 a month
image.caption: Food accounted for most of October's rise in the Lusaka basket, and the centre expects more as the dry spell continues.

body: The cost of meeting a Lusaka family's basic needs rose by K854.08 in October to K12,253.72, the Jesuit Centre for Theological Reflection said in its monthly Basic Needs and Nutrition Basket, published on Tuesday 10 November. That is a 7.5% jump in a single month, Zambia Monitor reported, and most of it came from food: the food component rose from K4,574.79 to K5,339.52. News Diggers reported that the centre's executive director, Fr Daniel Mutale, attributed the rise mainly to vegetables and bananas, and the Daily Nation gave the figures: a 40kg bag of vegetables went from K763.97 to K1,122.57 and a kilogram of bananas from K18.95 to K29.06.

Across the 16 districts the centre monitors, the October basket averaged K7,660.84. Lusaka was the most expensive at K12,253.72, followed by Ndola at K10,449.46 and Solwezi at K9,646.87; Chinsali was the cheapest at K6,043.67, News Diggers and Zambia Monitor reported. The centre expects prices to keep rising while the El Niño-linked dry spell continues. It also noted that headline inflation has fallen to 6.3% in October from 11.2% in December 2025 without households feeling much relief.

body.text: The budget, read from the bottom

body: Much of the centre's statement was about the K284.8 billion 2027 budget presented on 6 November. The Daily Nation reported Fr Mutale's argument that the government should have imposed a windfall tax on high copper profits rather than add to the burden on citizens; that formal and semi-formal workers are taxed hardest because they are easy to find through the NAPSA, ZRA and NHIMA databases; that mining agreements should be negotiated while prices are favourable; and that debt service now exceeds spending on health, education, agriculture and social protection combined. Zambia Monitor reported the centre's specific objections: raising VAT from 16% to 16.5% and increasing the mobile-money levy will push up the price of essentials for low-income households, and the income-tax-free threshold stays at K5,100, where it has been since 2024, even as a new 39.5% rate applies to monthly income above K37,000.

The centre did find things to welcome, Zambia Monitor reported: the social cash transfer rises from K400 to K450 a month (K600 to K650 for households with a person with a disability), social protection spending goes from K15.6 billion to K16.2 billion and coverage from 1.5 million to more than 1.6 million households, disaster risk management funding rises from K81.4 million to K316.5 million, and 1,400 megawatts of non-hydro generation is planned. But K450 is 3.7% of the Lusaka basket, the centre pointed out, and there is no money for the Food Security Pack in 2027, which it called a major concern.

body.text: actually lowers the cost of living for the poor
body.attribution: What Fr Daniel Mutale, executive director of the JCTR, said a budget should do, in the centre's statement of Tuesday 10 November as quoted by Zambia Monitor

body: PricewaterhouseCoopers reached a similar conclusion from the other end of the income scale, News Diggers reported on Wednesday: Zambians will feel the budget through shopping, because the half-point VAT rise, the higher top PAYE rate and the mobile-money levy may each look small but add up at the till. The firm urged the government to set a clear, time-bound plan to settle K60 billion in outstanding VAT refunds. The budget targets K233.7 billion in domestic revenue, up from a K253 billion total budget in 2026.

The government's case for the tax measures was made at the budget symposium on Monday and in Parliament on Tuesday: domestic revenue must rise to 23.6% of GDP by 2029, Mr Nkulukusa said, and Zambia itself, in Dr Musokotwane's words to the House, is an example of a country that has become better off after an IMF programme, News Diggers reported.

stories.title: 'A true leader should never take people for granted': from his Choma farm, Hichilema tells MPs who wanted ministries to be grateful for their seats and the party to stay united
stories.excerpt: Speaking to supporters who gathered at his farm in Choma on Tuesday 10 November, at the start of a ten-day working holiday in Southern Province, the President told elected leaders and appointees to remain loyal and respectful to the UPND structures that built the party, and told MPs unhappy at being passed over for Cabinet to appreciate that voters elected them, citing the Choma MP Cornelius Mweetwa's decade in the seat. A public thank-you rally in Choma follows on Friday.

image.label: Ten days in the south
image.caption: A working holiday with a message for the party: the structures come first, and a seat in Parliament is not a consolation prize.

body: President Hakainde Hichilema used a ten-day working holiday in Southern Province to speak to his own party. Addressing residents and supporters who had gathered to welcome him at his farm in Choma District on Tuesday 10 November, he told UPND elected leaders and ministerial appointees to remain loyal and respectful to the party structures, and said that holding public office should not make anyone forget the people who built the party, the Times of Zambia reported on Wednesday.

News Diggers reported the sharper edge of the same remarks. The President said elected leaders should not take people for granted, because people have their own views, feelings and opinions, and he told MPs unhappy at not having been named ministers to appreciate that voters had chosen them. He pointed to the Choma MP, Cornelius Mweetwa, who has held the seat for more than ten years, as his example. He also asked UPND members to mobilise support more actively and to publicise the government's achievements, saying the party had learned lessons from the August election campaign.

body.text: a true leader should never take people for granted because they have their own views, feelings and opinions
body.attribution: President Hakainde Hichilema, speaking in Choma District on Tuesday 10 November, as quoted by News Diggers

body: The Times of Zambia reported that the President asked party members in the province to keep their structures functional and united, and announced a major public engagement in Choma on Friday to thank citizens for renewing the UPND's mandate. He said his main concern was the welfare of Zambians, especially children and orphans and their access to a good education, and that the public university planned for Choma would serve the whole country rather than Southern Province alone; every province, he said, deserved one. The visit includes public engagements and tours of development projects, the Times reported.

News Diggers framed the reference to Mr Mweetwa as a message to MPs who had hoped for ministerial jobs after the August election. Neither outlet reported a response from Mr Mweetwa or any other MP, and neither carried an opposition reaction.
The President's Southern Province programme runs for ten days, the Times of Zambia reported, with Friday's Choma rally the first fixed public event.

stories.title: 'Verification and recruitment can run together': Tonse says freezing teacher hiring in 2027 contradicts what the UPND once demanded of the PF; the Treasury says count first
stories.excerpt: Muhabi Lungu, acting secretary general of the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance, told Capital FM that the decision not to recruit teachers next year is a missed chance to bring the pupil-teacher ratio towards 1:25, that the UPND criticised the PF for exactly this, and that education's 13% of the 2027 budget falls short of the 20% benchmark. The Finance Minister said on ZNBC on Sunday that there is no plan to recruit in 2027 until deployment irregularities are resolved and the real staffing gaps are known.

image.label: No hiring in 2027
image.caption: The government says it must count before it recruits; the opposition says it can do both at once.

body: The opposition Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance has made the suspension of teacher recruitment its first line of attack on the 2027 budget. Its acting secretary general, Muhabi Lungu, speaking on Capital FM's Conversations with HOPE programme, called the decision a missed opportunity to address teacher shortages and improve the pupil-teacher ratio, The Zambian Observer reported on Wednesday 11 November. He said Zambia should be aiming for a ratio of between 1:25 and 1:30, and that classes of 100 or 150 pupils to a teacher undermine any teaching at all.

Mr Lungu's political point was that the UPND had attacked the Patriotic Front government over difficulties in recruiting teachers and was now taking the same approach itself. His practical point was that the government's stated reason for the freeze, a verification exercise, does not require one: in his words, as reported by the Observer, the government can conduct its verification exercise while continuing to recruit teachers. He questioned the roughly 13% of the 2027 budget allocated to education against the internationally advocated 20%, warned that growth in enrolment under free education must be matched by quality teaching, and said the suspension would slow youth employment in education and health. The alliance reserved a full assessment of the budget's third part pending technical analysis, saying it did not want to make uninformed pronouncements on matters that needed detailed economic analysis.

The policy itself was set out by the Minister of Finance and National Planning, Situmbeko Musokotwane, on ZNBC's Sunday Interview, News Diggers reported on Tuesday. Asked whether more teachers would be recruited in 2027, he answered plainly that there was no plan to do so next year, and tied the decision to irregularities in teacher deployment and to establishing the actual staffing gaps in schools before hiring again. In the same interview he said the government wanted to improve domestic tax collection and that Zambians might have been spoilt by years of donor support.

body.text: No, for next year there is no plan to recruit teachers.
body.attribution: Situmbeko Musokotwane, Minister of Finance and National Planning, on ZNBC's Sunday Interview on 8 November, as quoted by News Diggers

body: The two positions are not quite opposites. The Tonse argument is that redistribution and recruitment are not alternatives and can run in parallel; the Treasury's, as the minister put it on Sunday, is that it cannot know how many teachers to hire until it knows where the existing ones are and why deployment went wrong.
Neither report records a response from the Ministry of Education to Mr Lungu's remarks, and the education vote is still before the House as part of the 2027 estimates.

stories.title: Planning for a dry season: ZESCO maps 11,630MW by 2030 with hydro down to a third, Kapala tells the REA to connect paid-up customers, and Nkana Water warns Kitwe of rationing
stories.excerpt: With an El Niño dry spell forecast for the 2026/27 rains, three strands of the power-and-water story came together this week. ZESCO presented targets to more than double installed capacity from 5,220MW to 11,630MW by 2030, with solar rising to 4,126MW; the Electricity Minister, on his first visit to the Rural Electrification Authority, said paid-up customers must be connected without delay; and Nkana Water cut output at Bulangililo by 18% because the Kafue River is falling.

image.label: 5,220 to 11,630 megawatts
image.caption: ZESCO's 2030 mix would cut hydro to about a third of generation; the Kafue is already telling Kitwe's water company why that matters.

body: ZESCO says it is reshaping Zambia's generation mix so that another drought does not bring back the 20-hour power cuts of 2024. At a presentation reported by The Zambian Observer on Wednesday 11 November, the utility's Director of Transmission Operations and Trade, Lioko Sitali, set out targets to raise installed capacity from 5,220 megawatts today to 11,630MW by 2030. Solar would grow from a 2021 baseline of 88MW to 4,126MW, thermal from 515MW to 3,234MW, hydro from about 2,700MW to 3,970MW, and the first 200MW of wind would be added, with 100MW from biomass and other sources. Hydro's share of generation would fall from 82% in 2021 to about 34%, with solar at roughly 35%.

The Observer's account recalled how the last dry year unfolded: load shedding began at eight hours a day in March 2024, rose to twelve in May and eventually to between 19 and 20 hours, before new solar, thermal and independent projects allowed supply to stabilise in late 2025 and ZESCO to end nationwide load shedding in December 2025. The managing director, Justin Loongo, said the utility was assessing renewable technologies and financing models and that private participation and regional trading would be needed. The Electricity Minister, Peter Kapala, welcomed the projections and said he hoped the country would exceed the government's 10,000MW target and reach universal access, including rural areas, by 2030.

Mr Kapala took the access argument to the Rural Electrification Authority on a familiarisation visit reported by the Daily Nation on Wednesday. He told the authority to speed up connections, above all for customers who have already paid, saying delays undermine the government's connection subsidy, and asked it to open offices in every province. ZESCO, he said, should concentrate on generation and transmission while the REA leads rural electrification. The REA's chief executive, Alex Mbumba, said the authority had made more than 62,000 new connections this year against a target of 100,000, hoped to pass 75,000 by the end of the year, and was expanding mini-grids and solar home systems.

body.text: Those who have already paid for the service should be connected without unnecessary delays.
body.attribution: Peter Kapala, Minister of Electricity, during a familiarisation visit to the Rural Electrification Authority, as quoted by the Daily Nation

body: The drought risk is already showing in Kitwe's taps. News Diggers reported on Wednesday that Nkana Water and Sanitation Company may introduce rationing because the Kafue River, one of its main raw-water sources, is falling. The company presented a report on river levels to the Copperbelt Minister, Emmanuel Kasambo, on Monday, attributing the decline to El Niño, and said it had cut production at the Bulangililo treatment plant by 18%, from 95,000 to 78,000 cubic metres a day, to prevent cavitation in its pumps. Its corporate affairs manager, Mwaka Nakweti, said in a statement that rationing would be used to share what is available fairly. No rationing schedule had been published by Wednesday.

Zambia Monitor reported last week that the regional transmission line to Tanzania and Kenya, the other half of ZESCO's drought insurance, is due for commissioning on the Zambian side in the second quarter of 2029: 613km of line from Pensulo to Nakonde via Mpika and Kasama, financed by US$292 million in grants from the World Bank, the European Union and the United Kingdom, allowing up to 500MW to be traded.

stories.title: One goal to find on Sunday: Nouhoun Koné's 21st-minute strike gives Burkina Faso a 1–0 first-leg lead over Zambia's under-23s in Ouagadougou after a delayed flight
stories.excerpt: Chisi Mbewe's side had more of the ball but could not find an equaliser after Koné put the young Étalons ahead in the first half of Wednesday's second-round first leg of the 2027 U-23 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers. The return is at National Heroes Stadium in Lusaka on Sunday 15 November, the first international in Lusaka since CAF approved the venue; the winner over two legs goes into the final round, on the road to Egypt 2027 and the Los Angeles Olympics.

image.label: Burkina Faso 1, Zambia 0
image.caption: A single first-half goal separates the sides before Sunday's return leg in Lusaka.

body: Zambia's under-23 side lost the first leg of their second-round qualifier 1–0 to Burkina Faso at the Stade du 4-Août in Ouagadougou on Wednesday 11 November. Nouhoun Koné scored the only goal in the 21st minute, Pan Africa Football reported, and the hosts defended the lead for the rest of the match. The visitors, who had reached Ouagadougou after a difficult journey that included a flight delay, had slightly more possession and some attacking moments but did not equalise.

The tie is decided over two legs. The return is at National Heroes Stadium in Lusaka on Sunday 15 November, with a 13:00 GMT kick-off, Sport News Africa reported, so Zambia must overturn a one-goal deficit in front of their own crowd. ZamFoot reported earlier this month that CAF approved the Lusaka venue, which FAZ's general secretary, Charles Chakatazya, had welcomed as opening the way for international matches to return to the capital while the senior team remains in Ndola.

This is the penultimate round of qualifying for the 2027 U-23 Africa Cup of Nations in Egypt, Pan Africa Football reported in its round-up of Wednesday's eight first legs. The winners go into a final round of seven two-legged ties, and the top finishers in Egypt qualify for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic football tournament. Elsewhere on Wednesday, Kenya came from behind to beat Ivory Coast 2–1, Mali won 3–0 in Zimbabwe, Cameroon won 3–0 in Rwanda, Guinea won 1–0 in Botswana, Libya beat Ghana 1–0, Eswatini beat Algeria 2–1 and South Sudan drew 0–0 with Senegal. Niger advanced without playing after Equatorial Guinea withdrew.

Coach Chisi Mbewe named a final 22-man squad for the double-header after the Armenia-based midfielder Sabobo Banda was ruled out injured, Africa Top Sports reported before the trip; several players who might otherwise have been in George Lwandamina's senior squad for Friday's game against Burundi are with the under-23s instead, ZamFoot noted. A one-goal deficit is the smallest Zambia could have brought home from West Africa short of a draw; it is still a goal that has to be scored in front of a Lusaka crowd on Sunday.

stories.title: Friday the 13th in Ndola: Zambia, second in Group I on three points, meet bottom-placed Burundi without Daka, Banda and Lungu, with the return in Bujumbura four days later
stories.excerpt: The first of two AFCON qualifiers against Burundi kicks off at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium on Friday 13 November. Zambia have three points from a 3–1 defeat in Algeria and a 2–0 win over Togo; Burundi have one, from a 2–2 draw with Algeria after losing 1–0 in Lomé. Captain Fashion Sakala and the goalkeeping coach Kennedy Mweene arrived on Monday, Kings Kangwa is available only for Tuesday's return leg, and the team doctor says the three injured forwards' recovery runs past the seven-day limit.

image.label: Group I, matchday three
image.caption: Three points separate Zambia from Burundi before the double-header; a win on Friday would put the Copper Bullets level with Algeria at worst.

body: Zambia's camp in Ndola took its final shape this week before Friday's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against Burundi at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium. The captain, Fashion Sakala, arrived on Monday with several other foreign-based players and the goalkeeping coach Kennedy Mweene, the Daily Nation reported on Wednesday 11 November, and the Young Africans striker Albert Kangwanda had flown in from Dar es Salaam earlier in the week on the same flight as a Burundi defender, Derrick Mukombozi, who once played for Nkana, ZamFoot reported.

The injuries that reshaped the squad are settled. Patson Daka, Lameck Banda and Gamphani Lungu are out of both legs, and the interim coach, George Lwandamina, has called up Edward Chilufya from Israel, Derrick Bulaya of Green Eagles and Prince Mumba, who plays in Iraq, News Diggers and the Daily Nation reported. The team doctor, George Magwende, said all three recovery periods went beyond the seven-day threshold for selection; News Diggers reported that Daka's injury is to his right ankle. Kings Kangwa has completed his suspension but is not eligible until the return leg in Bujumbura on Tuesday 17 November.

Zambia are second in Group I with three points from two games, having lost 3–1 away to Algeria and beaten Togo 2–0 in Ndola, the Daily Nation and ZamFoot reported. Algeria lead on four points, Togo also have three, and Burundi are bottom on one. Burundi opened their campaign with a 1–0 defeat in Lomé in September after conceding an early goal, then drew 2–2 with Algeria in Bujumbura on 29 September after giving up a late equaliser, the Daily Nation reported in its account of the visitors' departure for Zambia. Their squad, nicknamed the Intamba m'Urugamba, draws on clubs in the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden, Rwanda, Tanzania, Mozambique, Canada, Algeria and Kenya.

The game is in Ndola rather than Lusaka because the deadline for meeting CAF's venue conditions could not be met in time to move it, FAZ's general secretary, Charles Chakatazya, said earlier this month, ZamFoot reported; the under-23 side's second leg at Heroes on Sunday is the first step back towards the capital. The finals, branded AFCON PAMOJA 2027, will be played in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania from 19 June to 17 July 2027.

What the two Burundi games will settle is whether a group that looked like a three-way contest between Algeria, Togo and Zambia after two rounds stays that way. The Daily Nation's assessment on Wednesday was that the camp is taking shape and strength; the three forwards it has lost are the reason that is an assessment rather than a certainty.

stories.title: 'Happy heavenly 70th birthday, Dad': Tasila Lungu marks the day her father would have turned seventy, seventeen months after his death and with his remains still in South Africa
stories.excerpt: Edgar Chagwa Lungu, Zambia's sixth president, would have been 70 on Wednesday 11 November. His daughter, the former Chawama MP Tasila Lungu, wrote that his love and lessons were still with the family every day. The Zambian Observer noted that more than a year after his death in South Africa on 5 June 2025 his remains have not been buried; South Africa's Supreme Court of Appeal ruled in June that the family, not the Zambian government, decides where and how that happens.

image.label: 11 November 1956
image.caption: A birthday marked online by a daughter, and a burial still unresolved seventeen months after a former president's death.

body: Wednesday 11 November would have been the seventieth birthday of Edgar Chagwa Lungu, who was President of Zambia from 2015 to 2021 and died in South Africa on 5 June 2025. His daughter Tasila Lungu, the former Chawama MP, marked the day with a social media post in which she wrote that she missed him and that the love and lessons he gave her and her siblings were still with them every single day, The Zambian Observer reported. She signed off with a birthday wish to her father in heaven.

body.attribution: Tasila Lungu, in a social media post on Wednesday 11 November, as quoted by The Zambian Observer

body: The Observer's own note on the anniversary, published early on Wednesday, recorded the unresolved matter behind the tributes: more than a year after his death, the former president's remains are still in South Africa, and the question of his final resting place continues to draw public attention. The comments beneath both pieces, the Observer's readers arguing over the family's handling of the funeral, were a small sample of a dispute that has run since the week he died.

The legal position was settled, at least in South Africa, on 23 June 2026, when the Supreme Court of Appeal ruled that Mr Lungu's family should decide where and how he is buried, Reuters reported in a story carried by Polity. The judgment overturned a lower court's order that would have allowed the Zambian government to repatriate the body for a state funeral, finding that Zambia had not shown a legal right under South African law to override the family's wishes and that the evidence showed continuing negotiations rather than a concluded agreement. The government had wanted a burial at the site in Lusaka reserved for former presidents; the family preferred a private burial in South Africa and had said Mr Lungu would not have wanted his successor and long-time rival, President Hakainde Hichilema, at his funeral. South Africa's government said it would respect the family's wishes while regarding a state burial in Zambia as the best outcome.

Earlier in June, before that ruling, Ms Lungu had written that the family was still waiting for a chance to bury her father the way he wished and that the pain of his loss remained raw, News Diggers reported at the time. None of this week's reports says that a burial has since taken place or been scheduled, and neither the family nor the government was reported to have said anything new on the subject on Wednesday.

Mr Lungu led Zambia from 2015 to 2021 and died in South Africa, where he had gone for medical treatment, Reuters reported. His years in office are still argued over in Zambian politics as hotly as his burial, and Wednesday's birthday, marked by his daughter with a few lines online, was a reminder that the second argument has not ended.

analysis.title: Weight or admissibility: why Friday's ruling matters beyond one flash disk
analysis.body: The State's second objection looks procedural, but the question underneath it is one the High Court will have to answer for every constitutional application that follows. The State says a video on a flash disk must be authenticated under Section 9 of the Electronic Communications and Transactions Act before a court may look at it, and that an affidavit in reply cannot introduce new material. The applicants say a flash disk is a document under the Evidence Act, that an affidavit sworn before a Commissioner for Oaths is properly before the court, and that doubts about a recording's provenance go to how much weight it carries, not whether it can be seen. If the panel agrees with the State, the bail application will be argued without the footage the defence says explains why the accused went to the United Nations rather than a police station. If it agrees with the applicants, the State's flight-risk argument will be answered on the record by a video it has not been able to examine. Either way, Friday's ruling is the first time this court will say how electronic evidence enters a constitutional bail hearing. The 18 have now been in custody for nearly three months without that hearing starting; that fact does not change whichever way the ruling goes.

analysis.title: Two readings of the same budget: the Treasury's arithmetic and the JCTR's basket
analysis.body: The Finance Minister's debt statement and the Jesuit centre's cost-of-living report describe the same economy from opposite ends. The Treasury's story is of a balance sheet repaired: external debt down 5% in six months, US$275 million saved on a 2053 bond, a new IMF programme at staff level and domestic revenue heading for 23.6% of GDP. The JCTR's is of a Lusaka household that needed K854 more in October than in September just to stand still, and faces half a point more VAT and a higher mobile-money levy under the budget proposals. Both are true; the dispute is over sequencing. The government's case, as the minister set it out on Sunday and Tuesday, is that years of donor support are over and services must be paid for from domestic taxes; inflation's fall from 11.2% to 6.3% is the backdrop it points to. The centre's and PwC's case is that the people easiest to tax are formal workers and small traders, that a windfall levy on copper would have spread the load, and that K60 billion in unpaid VAT refunds is itself a tax on business. What to watch: the IMF board in December, whether the Food Security Pack reappears in the estimates, and the November basket, due in early December, which will show whether the dry-season spike in vegetables was a blip or a trend.

analysis.title: El Niño is a 2029 problem being managed with 2026 tools
analysis.body: ZESCO's plan to reach 11,630 megawatts by 2030 with hydro at a third of the mix is the right answer to the wrong year. The dry spell forecasters expect this rainy season would show in the reservoirs in 2027, before most of that solar and thermal capacity exists and before the line to Tanzania opens in 2029. What the utility can do now is what it did in late 2025, when new solar, thermal and independent projects let it end nationwide load shedding in December: keep every new plant feeding the grid and buy in what it cannot generate. Nkana Water's 18% cut at Bulangililo shows how early the water side of a drought arrives; the Kafue at Kitwe is falling in November, not March. The minister's push on the REA is about something different, connections for people who have already paid, but it points at the same constraint: a grid can be expanded on paper faster than it can be built. Two things will tell whether this season is managed better than 2024. First, whether ZESCO publishes a contingency schedule before the rains fail rather than after. Second, how much of the 2030 capacity reaches financial close in the next twelve months. The targets are credible; the calendar is the problem.
